Leasing Company Southeast, LLC, 722 F.3d 609 (4th Cir. 2013). A 
unanimous panel of the D.C. Circuit had reached the same conclusion in a 
somewhat more complex case involving the Block, Flynn and Griffin 
appointments. Noel Canning u. NLRB, 705 F.3d 490 (D.C. Cir. 2013).
The complexity of the D.C. Circuit case arose because of the following 
unusual scenario. In December 2011, with the end of the first session of the 
112th Congress approaching, the Republican House majority deployed a 
maneuver to prevent—^they hoped—the Democratic-majority Senate from 
having a long enough intersession recess to permit recess appointments to 
occur. They exercised the House’s right under Article I, section 5 of the 
Constitution to prevent the Senate from adjourning for periods longer than 
three days. As a result, between December 17, 2011, and January 23, 2012, 
the Senate convened every three days for “pro forma sessions,” typically 
lasting only a couple of minutes, if that, during which the only business 
conducted—often by a single Senator—was simply a call to order and an 
adjournment until the next pro forma session. These “gatherings” were 
conducted pursuant to a Senate unanimous consent resolution that had 
provided there would be “no business conducted” during such sessions. As 
viewed, therefore, by President Obama, and pursuant to advice firom the 
Justice Department’s Office of Legal Counsel, the pro forma sessions left 
unchanged the reahty that the Senate was unavailable from January 3 to 
January 23, 2012, to act on nominations. The President took the legal 
position that the pro forma sessions left the “recess”—and his recess 
appointments power—^intact.
The D.C. Circuit held, however, that the appointments were 
impermissible intrasession appointments. Two of the three judges went 
further to hold that the recess appointments power existed only for offices 
that first became vacant during an intersession recess of the Senate. 
Having decided the case on this basis, the court gave no consideration to 
the legal status of the Senate’s pro forma sessions. Because the case 
involved only the president’s NLRB recess appointees, the court’s judgment 
did not reach a fourth Obama action on January 4, 2012—the recess 
appointment of Richard Cordray to be director of the Consumer Finance 
Protection Bureau (CFPB).
The Supreme Court unanimously upheld the judgment of the D.C. 
Circuit but spht 5—4 as to rationale. The majority, per Justice Breyer, re Red 
on its interpretation of longstanding historical practice to hold that 
presidents are entitled to use their recess appointment powers during 
either intersession or intrasession recesses, and that recess appointments 
could be used even to fill vacancies that originated while the Senate was in 
session. Based on that same history, however, the Court held that only 
periods of adjournment lasting at least ten days counted as “recesses”
